title: Triangles with integer exradii and inradius n/4
connection: For any triangle 1/r = 1/r_a + 1/r_b + 1/r_c, and every positive triple (r_a,r_b,r_c) is realised by a unique triangle (Ravi substitution). So ES(n) ⇔ there is a triangle with integer exradii and inradius exactly n/4.
why: An exact, unrestricted Euclidean-geometry form. Triangle geometry has its own integrality theory (Heronian triangles, integer exradii), and a Heronian strengthening gives testable variants.
first_step: Verify the 'any positive exradii ⟹ triangle' claim; then compute, over ES solutions for p ≤ 10⁴, how often e₂(x,y,z) is a perfect square (rational semiperimeter) and search literature for 'integer exradii triangles'.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0028] Test the stronger variant 'exists a Heronian triangle with integer exradii and inradius n/4' for n ≤ 10⁴; if it holds broadly, rational parametrisations of Heronian triangles give new families.
repo_note: Triangle/inradius reformulations examined; integer-exradius triangles not analysed for ES.

title: Triangles with integer altitudes and inradius n/4 (the x > n/2 subfamily)
connection: 1/h_a + 1/h_b + 1/h_c = 1/r. A triangle with altitudes x,y,z exists iff the reciprocals satisfy the triangle inequality, i.e. iff x > n/2 for the smallest x. So 'ES with x ∈ (n/2, 3n/4]' ⇔ a triangle with integer altitudes and inradius n/4.
why: It is a natural geometric sub-variant. It turns out to be false at every prime p ≡ 1 (4) (see first step), which is a clean calibration: the triangle inequality on reciprocals is incompatible with ES at hard primes.
first_step: DONE (cheap test, scripts/z52b_translate_cheap.py): the variant FAILS for EVERY prime p ≡ 1 (4) (checked < 1500 after a reviewer caught an ordering bug in the first script; proof: if all of x,y,z > p/2 then x,y < p, so z = kp with 4k ≡ 1 (mod p) and k ≤ (p+1)/4, impossible for p ≡ 1 (4)). So the integer-altitude strengthening is false at all hard primes; record it as a dead variant.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0352] For p ≤ 10⁴, classify ES solutions by whether 1/x < 1/y + 1/z holds (altitude-realisable) and check if every p has a realisable one.
[signature-0055] For hard primes ≤ 10⁵, compute the fraction of ES solutions satisfying the triangle inequality on (1/x,1/y,1/z); look up 'triangles with integer altitudes' parametrisations.
[signature-0340] Derive the altitude/inradius identity under rational side-area normalization and check which integral triangle families yield denominators matching 4/n.
[signature-0356] Homogenize the triangle identity and ES surface side by side and identify whether either has a birational map preserving positive rational points.

title: Cubic polynomial T²(T − s) + e(T − n/4) with three positive integer roots
connection: x,y,z are the roots of T³ − sT² + e₂T − e₃ with 4e₃ = n·e₂, i.e. of 4T²(T−s) + e₂(4T − n). So ES(n) ⇔ for some (s, e₂) this cubic splits completely over ℤ with positive roots.
why: It is a 'totally split specialisation' problem for a 2-parameter family of cubics. Hilbert-irreducibility counting and 'polynomials with many split values' (Schinzel-type) are the native field.
first_step: Compute the Galois group over Q(s,e) (generic S₃) and the discriminant surface. Check whether split points lie on a subvariety with a parametrisation (they should be exactly U_n).

title: Slice-rank of the ES 'certificate tensor' modulo q
connection: The cap-set proof bounds sets avoiding a pattern via the slice rank of the pattern's indicator tensor. Consider the tensor T(u, B, C) = 1[4uBC − u − B ≡ p (mod q)] over F_q³; its slice rank bounds how large a product set of parameter values can avoid certificates mod q.
why: Gives polynomial-method bounds on 'certificate-avoiding parameter sets' mod q, a local statement with sharp constants.
first_step: Compute the slice rank (or a polynomial-method upper bound) of T for small q and compare with the largest avoiding product sets found by search.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0069] Compute the slice rank of T_n(x,y,z) = 1[4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)] over 𝔽_ℓ for small ℓ and compare with the size of solution-free sets.
